prompt:
Produce one block about the image, in exactly this format:

<CAPTION>
one paragraph of description
</CAPTION>

<CAPTION> rules:
- One paragraph of 400-1024 characters (roughly 4-9 sentences), on a single line. Stop at the upper bound: the reply is truncated there, and a caption cut mid-sentence is thrown away.
- Order the content: main subject; setting and background; composition and camera angle when clear; lighting; only short, prominent, clearly legible text when useful, quoted verbatim inside double quotes.
- Mention colour and surface/material details for the main subject and other prominent objects when they are clearly visible and useful. Omit uncertain details; do not infer material from colour, lighting or context.
- Describe clearly visible spatial relationships between main subjects (position, overlap or contact) when they help explain the scene. Omit them when they are unclear or irrelevant.
- Describe only what is visible. Do not speculate about anything outside the frame.
- Do not name or guess the artist, character, series or studio. A signature or watermark is visible text, not proof of authorship; quote it only if prominent and useful, and never resolve it into a name. Trusted artist metadata is added separately by the annotation system.
- When clearly distinguishable, name the overall art style and medium in one clause (anime illustration, watercolour, oil painting, 3D render, photograph); mention line work and finish only when clearly visible.
- English only, plain prose: no markdown, no bullet points, no headings, no "Caption:" prefix.
- Quote only short, clearly legible text that is prominent and useful for understanding the image, verbatim in its original script.
- never translate the text, and never romanise non-Latin scripts.
- Keep original punctuation and reading order within a quotation. Omit illegible text; never guess missing characters or add [unreadable] placeholders.
- Speech bubbles and dense print are visual elements only, even when readable. Mention their presence in one brief clause if visually important; do not quote, paraphrase or summarize their contents, count every bubble or list each text region. Only a standalone sign, title or other prominent text subject may supply one short, clearly legible quotation.
- Do not describe the font or layout unless the text itself is the subject.
- A quoted date, year or timestamp is visible text only; never use it to infer when the work was made or which era its style belongs to.
- When the image has no text, leave text out of the caption entirely.

Output the CAPTION block and nothing else.

Final instruction: For any image containing speech bubbles, the entire caption must contain ZERO words or paraphrases from those bubbles. Describe the visible people, colors, clothing and setting instead. A short phrase such as "speech bubbles surround the subject" is enough. Do not mention absent text, signatures or watermarks. Keep the entire description under 100 words.
raw:
<CAPTION>
A stylized cartoon figure with a brown bob haircut, a red sleeveless top, and blue pants stands centered on a green ground against a light blue background. Speech bubbles surround the figure on both sides. The figure has a simple smiling face with black dot eyes and no visible hands or feet. The art style is flat vector illustration with bold black outlines and solid color fills.
</CAPTION>

prompt: Write <CAPTION> followed by a concise English description and </CAPTION>. Use 3 sentences, under 90 words. Describe the subject, colors, clothing, setting and style. If speech bubbles are present, only say that they are present; NEVER report what they say. Quote text only on a standalone sign. Do not invent signatures, names or background stories.
raw: <CAPTION> A simple cartoon figure in a red top and blue pants stands on green ground against a light blue background. Speech bubbles surround the figure. The style is minimalist with flat colors and basic shapes. </CAPTION>

prompt:
# Captioning format:

Return exactly one valid JSON object and nothing else. Use double-quoted keys and string values; do not add Markdown fences, comments, ellipses, or trailing commas. Use this shape:
{
  "General": "Briefly describe the overall composition and setting.",
  "character_1": "Describe the first visible human or humanlike character.",
  "image_effects": "Describe distinct visual effects, or None.",
  "texts": "None",
  "watermarks": "None"
}
Add one character_N field for each clearly visible human or humanlike character; omit character fields when none are present. Do not put a guessed name in a key. Keep descriptions concise and literal. Use "None" for absent image_effects, texts, or watermarks.

# Characters on picture:
Do not guess names for characters, artists, series or studios. Do not infer authorship from a signature or watermark. The annotation system adds any trusted artist metadata separately; do not write artist attribution or an artist-style prefix yourself.

# Visible text:
Focus on visible subjects and setting. For dense dialogue, many speech bubbles, repeated labels or tiny background print, briefly note their presence only when visually important; do not transcribe or retell their contents, count every bubble or list each text region.
Quote only short, prominent, clearly legible text that helps explain the image, keeping its original script and punctuation; never translate or romanise it. If text itself is the main subject, quote at most one short prominent phrase. Omit illegible text without guessing characters or adding unreadable placeholders. Put text details only in texts and watermark details only in watermarks; do not repeat them in General or character fields. A visible date or year does not establish when the artwork was made.

# Subject and hair boundary:
Call a subject a person only when it is a real person or a drawn humanlike character.
Describe animals, fur, manes, plush toys, dolls, mannequins, statues, sculptures and ordinary
objects as those kinds of subjects. Do not mistake animal fur or a mane, a doll's wig, or carved
hair on a statue for human scalp hair.
An upright, clothed or animal-headed creature is still an animal unless a separate human or clearly
humanlike drawn person is visible. Do not treat ears, horns, muzzles, feathers, scales or fur as
human scalp hair.
When a person is present, use girl, boy, woman, man or person in the first sentence of that
person's description. Do not turn a person's clothing, accessories, facial hair, lighting or
the background into hair.


Final instruction: For any image containing speech bubbles, the entire caption must contain ZERO words or paraphrases from those bubbles. Describe the visible people, colors, clothing and setting instead. A short phrase such as "speech bubbles surround the subject" is enough. Do not mention absent text, signatures or watermarks. Keep the entire description under 100 words.
